Sir Christopher Lee and Edgar Allan Poe went way back. Or at least they went as far back as 1969, the year of The Oblong Box, a loose and lurid film adaptation of the eponymous story starring Lee and the also Poe-associated Vincent Price. Lee plays the doctor to whom a gang of grave-robbers delivers Price’s character, an Englishman disfigured in a voodoo ceremony who fakes his own death in order to escape the captivity of his brother. Whatever its entertainment value, the picture doesn’t rank especially high in the canon of Poe adaptations. Nor, for that matter, does the original story rank alongside works like “The Pit and the Pendulum,” “The Fall of the House of Usher,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” or “The Black Cat.”

You can hear Lee himself read all those macabre, imaginative stories and others besides in the YouTube playlist above. Some of the recordings come from Christopher Lee Reads Edgar Allan Poe Tales of Horror, the 1979 budget-label cassette previously featured here on Open Culture. Others include Lee’s performances of “The Masque of the Red Death,” “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “Hop-Frog,” and “The Murders in the Rue Morgue,” which is commonly credited with launching the entire genre of detective fiction.

Though now most widely remembered as a horror actor, the prolific Lee proved commanding in a variety of genres: in the final decade of his life, he appeared in numerous crime pictures, adaptations of The Golden Compass and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, and several Star Wars and Lord of the Rings movies.

Not that he’d left Poe behind. Among the last credits Lee racked up in his lifetime is Extraordinary Tales, from 2013, a five-story anthology film in which he narrates “The Fall of the House of Usher.” Though British, his distinctive manner and slightly mid-Atlantic accent were as versatile on the screen as they were in readings of Poe, whose writing dates from a time when more than a few Americans still considered literature itself an import from across the pond. This Halloween, if you don’t have the hours free for a complete listen-through of the playlist do consider at least putting on “The Raven.” It remains a matter of debate among Poe enthusiasts to what extent Lee’s delivery of “nevermore” really captures the spirit of the poem, but it would be hard to imagine a more appropriate figure to preside over All Hallows’ Eve.
